## Q1

```{r}
birthday_sim = function(n) {

  if (!is.numeric(n) || n < 1) {
    stop("n_room should be a positive number")
  }

  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)

  repeated_bday = length(unique(birthdays)) < n

  repeated_bday
}
```

```{r}
birthday_sim_df =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(res = map_lgl(group_size, birthday_sim)) |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(prob = mean(res))

birthday_sim_df
```
Plot
```{r}
birthday_sim_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = prob)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probab that 2+ People Share a Birthday by Group Size ",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Probability of a Shared Birthday"
  )
```
Plotting the probability of sharing the same birthday as a function of group size results in a signmoidal curve. Generally the probability of sharing a birthday increases as group size increases peaking at almost 1 or 100% when group size is 50.The steepest increase in probability of atleast two people sharing a birthday is between group size 10 to 30 people. 

## Q2
```{r}
full_df =
  tibble(
    files = list.files("data/"),
    path = str_c("data/", files)
  ) |>
  mutate(data = purrr::map(path, read_csv)) |> 
  unnest(data) |>
  mutate(files = str_remove(files, ".csv")) |>
  separate(files, into = c("arm_type", "subject_id"), sep = "_") |> 
  mutate(
    arm_type = case_match(
      arm_type,
      "con" ~ "control",
      "exp" ~ "experimental"
    )) |> 
  pivot_longer(
  starts_with("week_"),
  names_to = "week",
  names_prefix = "week_",
  values_to = "observation"
)
```
Plot 

```{r}
full_df |>  
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, group = subject_id, color = arm_type)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_path() + 
  facet_grid(~arm_type) +
labs(title = "Observations over 8 Weeks by Study Arm")
```

Based on the two graphs, observations in the control arm appear to stay relatively constant over the 8 weeks, with values ranging between about −2.5 and 5.0. In comparison, observations in the experimental arm increase over the 8-week period. At week 1, the range is about −1 to 3.75, but by week 8 this range shifts upward to about 3.25 to 7. This highlights how observation values increase over the 8 weeks in the experimental arm, whereas in the control arm they stay relatively consistent over time, which suggests the experimental treatment is associated with an increase in observations.

```{r}
sim = function(n = 30, mu = 0, sigma = 5) {
  
  sim_data = tibble(
    x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  )
  
  sim_data |> 
    pull(x) |> 
    t.test(mu = 0) |> 
    broom::tidy() |> 
    select(mu_hat = estimate, p_value = p.value)
}
sim_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |> 
  mutate(output = map(true_mu, \(m) sim(mu = m))) |>  
  unnest(output)
```

Plot 

```{r}
sim_results_df |> 
  group_by(true_mu) |> 
  summarize(power = mean(p_value < 0.05)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Power of a One-Sample T-test by True Mean",
    x = "True μ",
    y = "Power"
  )
```

As effect size increases from 0 to 6, the power increases as a result. The relationship between power and effect size follows a sigmoidal curve. At an effect size of 0, power is about 0.05, which equals alpha, because the null is true and every rejection is a false positive. Power then rises steeply, from about 0.19 at μ = 1 to 0.56 at μ = 2 and 0.88 at μ = 3, and reaches its maximum value of 1 from about μ = 4 onward. This shows that larger effect sizes are easier to detect.

```{r}
sim_results_df |> 
  group_by(true_mu) |> 
  summarize(
    all_samples = mean(mu_hat),
    rejected_only = mean(mu_hat[p_value < 0.05])
  ) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    -true_mu,
    names_to = "samples",
    values_to = "avg_mu_hat"
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = avg_mu_hat, color = samples)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Average μ̂ vs. True μ: All vs. Rejected Samples",
    x = "True μ",
    y = "Average μ̂",
    color = "Samples"
  )
```
No the sample average of mu across tests for which the null is  rejected is not approximately equal to the true value of mu for all values of true mu. For smaller true mu values (1–3), it is not equal: the average of mu hat for rejected tests is higher than the true mu.

For true mu values above 4, the sample average of mu  across tests for which the null is rejected IS approximately equal to the true value of mu. In the graph, this is where the yellow and purple lines meet. 

The gap between the two lines comes from how the test decides to reject. With n = 30 and σ = 5, the standard error of μ̂ is about 5/√30 ≈ 0.91. A two-sided t-test at α = 0.05 therefore needs μ̂ to land about 2 standard errors from zero, roughly 1.9, before it rejects. When the true μ is 1, a typical estimate doesn’t get that far, so the only datasets that make it into the “rejected” group are the ones that overshot. That’s why the yellow point at μ = 1 sits at about 2.25, more than double the truth. The same thing happens, less dramatically, at μ = 2 (≈ 2.6) and μ = 3 (≈ 3.2). Once μ reaches 4, almost every dataset clears the 1.9 threshold, so being rejected says little about whether a sample was unusually high. The rejected group is basically all the samples, and the two lines overlap. At μ = 0, the rejected samples split between large positive and large negative estimates. These mostly offset each other, so the yellow point (≈ 0.3) stays close to 0. In short, keeping only the significant results selects the samples that overestimated μ, and that matters most when power is low.
